title: What's the deal with indigo?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore indigo as a dye and pigment: how blue was hard to get in the ancient world (woad and Indigofera plants, fermentation process, Indus Valley use), the spice-trade and Marco Polo and Vasco da Gama era of indigo as "blue gold," and the link to slavery in the American South through Eliza Lucas Pinckney's indigo plantations and Georgia lifting its slavery ban in 1751. They then cover the synthetic indigo invention by Adolf von Baeyer (after William Perkins's synthetic mauve), the collapse of natural indigo production, and modern environmental damage from denim dyeing and proposed bacterial (genetically engineered E. coli) indigo production. The episode ends with a listener mail correction about New Hampshire's "Live Free or Die" motto versus Maine.
topics: live free or die New Hampshire motto

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Live show dates, snack talk about ramen, beef jerky and food weighing, and the hosts introduce the topic of indigo.

segments.title: Natural color and the blue problem
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how nearly all historical dyes came from plants, insects and sea snails, and why blue was hard to get naturally. They discuss blue foods and the idea that there are no true blue foods.

segments.title: Woad and Indigofera: early sources of indigo
segments.summary: Indigo came from woad in Europe and from the Indigofera plant in India and South America. Neither plant yields dye easily, and the earliest blue dye traces to about five thousand years ago. The Indus Valley civilization used indigo.

segments.title: Trade, Marco Polo, and Vasco da Gama
segments.summary: Indigo was traded at high cost along land routes. Europeans thought it was a mineral until Marco Polo reported it came from a plant. Vasco da Gama's sea route to India and China lowered prices, and indigo became known as blue gold.

segments.title: How indigo is made by fermentation
segments.summary: The process starts by fermenting Indigofera leaves to release the precursor indican, which splits into indoxyl and glucose. Air oxidation forms indigo, which settles, is filtered, and is dried into cakes. Natural indigo must be applied repeatedly to bind to fabric.

segments.title: Brief aside on jeans styles
segments.summary: A short tangent about the hosts' jeans and cutoff shorts.

segments.title: Eliza Lucas Pinckney and indigo slavery in the American South
segments.summary: Eliza Lucas Pinckney grew indigo on plantations near Charleston, South Carolina, using knowledge from enslaved Africans. The indigo boom increased slavery, and Georgia lifted its slavery ban in 1751 to grow indigo. The Revolutionary War hurt the indigo market.

segments.title: Synthetic indigo and the collapse of natural indigo
segments.summary: William Perkins's synthetic mauve came first, then Adolf von Baeyer developed synthetic indigo. Natural indigo production fell from about 19,000 to 1,000 tons within about fifteen years.

segments.title: Environmental cost of denim dyeing and bacterial indigo
segments.summary: Denim dyeing pollutes rivers, with mordants and chemical waste harming fish. Researchers have genetically engineered E. coli to produce the indigo precursor as a cleaner method, though scaling up remains a question.

segments.title: Closing reflections on ethical consumption
segments.summary: The hosts reflect that most products have some harmful practice in their supply chain and that partial good choices still matter.

segments.title: Listener mail: New Hampshire vs Maine motto
segments.summary: Listener John Cuneo corrects Josh that 'Live Free or Die' is New Hampshire's motto, not Maine's; Maine's motto is Dirigo. Josh says he was trolling and apologizes.
